result.summary: After a quarrel between Idmon and Idas is calmed by Orpheus' song, the Argo sails from Pagasae down the coast to Lemnos. There the women, who have killed their men, welcome the Argonauts, and Jason meets Queen Hypsipyle. Heracles at last rebukes the crew for lingering, and they depart.

scenes.title: Quarrel and Orpheus' Song
scenes.summary: Idas mocks the gods and Idmon rebukes him; Orpheus stops the strife with a song of creation and the early gods. The heroes pour libations and sleep.
scenes.stakes: Idas risks divine anger and a fight among the crew; the expedition's unity is at risk.

scenes.title: Departure of the Argo
scenes.summary: At dawn Tiphys rouses the crew and the Argo sails, watched by gods, nymphs and Chiron. Orpheus sings and fish follow; they stop at the tomb of Dolops.
scenes.stakes: The perilous voyage begins, and Jason leaves his homeland.

scenes.title: Sailing to Lemnos
scenes.summary: The ship passes many headlands and Mount Athos, reaching Lemnos by oar at nightfall.

scenes.title: The Women of Lemnos
scenes.summary: The narrator tells how Cypris' wrath led the women to slay all the men, sparing only Thoas. Fearing Thracians, they arm, but Aethalides persuades Hypsipyle to receive the Argonauts.
scenes.stakes: The women fear Thracian attack and retribution for their crime.

scenes.title: Assembly of the Lemnian Women
scenes.summary: Hypsipyle proposes sending gifts; Polyxo urges them to take the strangers as protectors and husbands. Iphinoe invites the Argonauts to the city.
scenes.stakes: The women's survival without men, and concealment of their crime.

scenes.title: Jason's Cloak and Spear
scenes.summary: The narrator describes Jason's embroidered cloak, Athena's gift, and Atalanta's spear. He walks to the city like a bright star.

scenes.title: Jason Meets Hypsipyle
scenes.summary: Hypsipyle tells a glossed version of the men's departure and offers Jason the kingship. He declines, and the crew accept hospitality.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks delay of the quest through hospitality and temptation.

scenes.title: Heracles Urges Departure
scenes.summary: Days of feasting pass until Heracles rebukes the crew. They prepare to leave, and Hypsipyle and Jason part with promises concerning a possible son.
scenes.stakes: The quest for the fleece is delayed; Hypsipyle faces losing her lover.

alias_notes.explanation: Pallas, Itonian and Tritonian are epithets of Athena.

notable_quotes.reason: Chiron's farewell cry to the departing Argonauts.
Orpheus' song of cosmic creation and separation of earth, heaven and sea.
Heracles shames the crew into resuming the quest.

analysis.text: Quarrels, delay and temptation test the crew's unity; Orpheus' song and Heracles' rebuke restore focus on the quest.
The Lemnian episode reflects Greek myth of a women-only community, and the cloak's images show Hellenistic poetic learning and ekphrasis.

legacy.text: The Lemnian women became a proverbial image of female violence, and Hypsipyle appears in later poets such as Statius and Ovid.

fun_facts.text: The poem names Aethalides' memory as surviving death, a detail linked to later tales of reincarnation.

language_notes.text: "Unmixed" wine means undiluted. The Greeks normally drank wine mixed with water, so drinking it neat signals recklessness and drunkenness.
The sons of Aloeus, Otus and Ephialtes, were giants who threatened to pile mountains up to heaven and attack the gods. Apollo killed them.
"Aphareian Iclas" is Idas, son of Aphareus. The text elsewhere calls him Idas; the name Iclas here is a variant.
This is an early theogony: Ophion and Eurynome ruled before Cronos and Rhea overthrew them, and Zeus was later hidden as a child in Crete.
"Poured them upon the burning tongues" refers to offering tongues of sacrificial victims burned on the fire, over which libations were poured.
Dodona was the oracle of Zeus in Epirus, famed for its sacred oak that spoke. The beam gives the Argo a prophetic voice.
Pouring wine on the sea was a libation, an offering to the gods for a safe voyage.
Pytho (Delphi), Ortygia (Delos) and the Ismenus near Thebes were all places of Phoebus Apollo's worship, famous for dances and song.
Itonian is an epithet of Athena, from Iton in Thessaly, where she was worshipped.
"Son of Oeagrus" is Orpheus, the legendary singer. Artemis is called child of a glorious sire, meaning Zeus.
Aphetae means roughly "the place of launching" or "departure", in Greek, explaining the beach's name.
Athos's shadow is said to reach Lemnos; the distance is given as a merchantship's sailing time until mid-day, a typical ancient way of measuring distance.
"Grudged her the honours due" means they withheld the worship and offerings owed to Cypris (Aphrodite).
"If haply he should escape" means in the hope that he might by chance survive.
"Kine" is an archaic plural for cattle; "works of Athena" means women's crafts such as spinning and weaving.
Thyiades are Bacchic women, frenzied followers of Dionysus, who rushed about in wild ecstatic bands.
The wand of Hermes is the herald's staff (caduceus), marking a messenger as protected. Aethalides, as Hermes' son, inherits the role.
Acheron is a river of the Underworld; his soul alternately dwelling below and in daylight reflects a myth of shifting between death and life.
"Straightway" means immediately; "spake" is the archaic past tense of speak.
"For need's sake" means because they need supplies; "wrought a terrible deed" alludes to the women's murder of their men, which the strangers must not learn of.
Polyxo is called Hypsipyle's "nurse" in the sense of an old woman who raised her; she is an elder of the community.
The Thracian host: Thracian men were the Lemnian women's neighbours, whose attack they fear in revenge for the killings, since the women had slain their own husbands.
"Put on the garment of earth" is a figure for dying and being buried; "meed" means due reward or share.
The Argonauts are misled: they take Thoas to be dead naturally, unaware that Hypsipyle secretly saved him while the women killed the other men.
Tritonian goddess: an epithet of Athena (Pallas), linked to Lake Triton in Libya, a place associated with her birth or upbringing in some traditions.
Keel-props are the supports on which a ship's keel rested during building; Athena guides the first construction of the Argo.
"Wouldst thou" is an archaic second person address to the reader, meaning 'you would'.
Cytherea is a name for Aphrodite (Venus), from the island of Cythera. Ares was her lover, so she holds his shield as a mirror.
Taphian raiders from the Taphian islands fought the sons of Electryon over cattle; the cattle raid led to the death of Electryon's sons.
Pelops won Hippodameia by a chariot race against her father Oenomaus, whose charioteer Myrtilus had sabotaged the axle.
Tityos assaulted Leto, mother of Apollo and Artemis; Apollo shoots him. Earth gave him 'second birth' because he was raised by her after his mother Elate died.
Phrixus escaped sacrifice on a golden-fleeced ram that spoke to him; this ram's fleece is the object of the Argonauts' quest.
"Fardarting" means a spear that can be thrown far. Atalanta was a famed huntress of Arcadia, where Maenalus is a mountain.
"Crafty words": Hypsipyle is about to give a deceptive account, hiding that the women killed their men.
"Sojourners" are temporary residents; she presents the men's absence as a farming stay in Thrace, not exile or death.
Cypris is a name for Aphrodite, goddess of love, said to have been born at or linked with Cyprus.
"Prerogative" means the special right or privilege of the king, here the royal power held by Thoas.
"Glozing over" means smoothing over or covering with fair words, here concealing the massacre.
"Wains" are wagons or carts; the women bring gifts to the shore in them.
Cypris is Aphrodite. She is acting for Hephaestus, whose wife she was, because the Lemnian women had neglected her worship and she had cursed them; the men's arrival ends that ruin.
"Steam of sacrifice" means the savoury smoke rising from roasting offerings. "Propitiated" means won the favour of.
The Argonauts are in exile or under guilt for killing kin; Heracles sarcastically asks if that is why they linger, when they should be heading home to Greece with the fleece.
The "fleece that moves of itself" is the Golden Fleece, the quest's goal. Heracles says it will not come to them by itself or by prayer.
"Forbode" means foresee or sense in advance; Hypsipyle senses Jason will not return to Lemnos.
Jason speaks ironically: "by the grace of Pelias" he can live at home, meaning Pelias has sent him on a perilous mission to get rid of him.
"Pelasgian Iolcus": Iolcus is Jason's home city in Thessaly. "Pelasgian" is an old poetic name for the pre-Greek peoples of Greece, here used for the region.

context_notes.text: Idmon is the Argonauts' seer, who foresees his own death on the voyage, so he speaks about doom with authority.
Orpheus, the legendary musician and poet, sings of cosmic origins, a traditional theme for epic and Orphic song.
The Cyclopes forged Zeus' thunderbolt, according to myth, which became his chief weapon and symbol of power.
Heracles is the strongest hero aboard, known for his club. His great weight makes the ship sink deeper.
Chiron was a wise centaur who lived on Pelion and trained heroes, including Achilles and Jason.
Achilles is Peleus' infant son, left in Chiron's care. Peleus is among the Argonauts.
Tiphys is the Argo's helmsman, valued for his skill in steering and reading the weather.
These are real places along the Thessalian and Macedonian coast, tracing the Argo's route north-east toward Lemnos.
Cypris is Aphrodite, goddess of love, named from Cyprus. Neglecting her honours was a typical cause of divine punishment.
The passage explains the name Sicinus, a typical Hellenistic aetiology, an account of how a place got its name.
Hypsipyle sits on her father Thoas's stone seat, showing she now rules Lemnos in his place.
The Minyae are the Argonauts, named after the Minyans, an ancient people of Greece from whom many of the heroes descended.
The Cyclops were smiths who forged Zeus's thunderbolts in myth.
Amphion and Zethus, twin sons of Antiope, built the walls of Thebes; Amphion's lyre music made the stones move into place.
Jason refuses Atalanta because her presence among the men might cause jealous quarrels.
Thoas was king of Lemnos, an island in the northern Aegean. Thrace lay on the mainland nearby.
In the wider story, Aphrodite afflicted the Lemnian women with a foul smell for neglecting her, and the men turned to Thracian captives.
The "illustrious son of Hera" is Hephaestus, god of the forge, who was honoured on Lemnos.
Heracles is the strongest of the Argonauts, and here he acts as the group's conscience against the idle stay.

literary_notes.text: Idas compares Idmon's prophecy to the idle wind, dismissing it as empty and insubstantial.
Orpheus' song of harmony answers the heroes' quarrel, showing music as a force that calms discord.
The song's charm lingers so strongly that the listeners stay entranced after the music has stopped, stressing Orpheus' power.
Jason's tears show his sorrow at leaving home, presenting him as feeling and uncertain rather than a confident leader.
The rowing in time to Orpheus' lyre is compared to a dance around Apollo's altar, making the labor graceful and almost sacred.
The wake compared to a path across a green plain turns the sea into land, a vivid contrast of white and green.
Gods and nymphs watching in wonder frame the voyage as a cosmic event that even immortals admire.
Fish following Orpheus' music like sheep following a piping shepherd conveys the charm of his song and the peacefulness of the scene.
The narrator breaks off to address the women directly, lamenting their blind jealousy and expressing sympathy and judgment together.
The armed women pouring onto the beach are compared to frenzied Thyiades, conveying their wild, dangerous energy.
The narrator interrupts himself with a rhetorical question, dropping a digression and reasserting control of the story.
The four white-haired virgin attendants add a vivid picture of age and dignity, supporting Polyxo's authority as an elder.
Polyxo asks whether oxen will plough themselves, mockingly stressing that the women cannot farm without men and need the strangers.
Death is imagined as clothing herself in earth, softening the idea of burial and showing Polyxo's calm acceptance.
Comparing the cloak's brightness to the sun exaggerates its splendour so that it seems too dazzling to look at.
The narrator describes a work of art so vividly that the images seem alive, as the ram seems to speak.
Jason's radiant walk is compared to a rising star admired by a lovesick girl, mixing admiration with longing and hinting at his romantic allure.
The warning of "crafty words" prepares the reader for Hypsipyle's partial, self-serving account.
Her phrasing, that some god gave the women courage to shut out their husbands, gently disguises the true violence the narrator reveals later.
The narrator steps in to expose her omission, so the reader knows more than Jason does.
The dancing maids crowding round Jason create a festive picture that contrasts with the hidden bloodshed on the island.
Heracles' string of sharp questions shames the crew without direct accusation, setting up the mocking tone.
Heracles sarcastically proposes leaving Jason behind as Lemnos's breeding stock, shaming him with the image of idle comfort.
The crew's silence shows Heracles' authority and their guilt.
The women pouring out around the men are compared to bees swarming over flowers, giving a sweet but busy, humming image of their clinging grief.
Hypsipyle's sad premonition that Jason will not return anticipates his later leaving of women behind, here and in Colchis.
